basics.name: Abhishek Ahirrao
basics.label: Platform & Software Engineer
basics.status: Looking for full-time platform, infrastructure or backend roles, starting 2027.
basics.summary: Platform engineer with 3.5 years at Quantiphi building self-service infrastructure, AWS data platforms and on-call tooling, now an MS Computer Science student at San José State University (class of 2027) working on LLM serving infrastructure, distributed systems and GPU programming.
intro: Most of what changed the world while I was growing up was software. Amazon changed how people shop. Social media changed how people talk, not always for the better. Now LLMs are changing how people work, and I wanted to help build that, not just watch it.

So far that has meant the unglamorous layer: the platforms, pipelines and infrastructure other people's work runs on. I spent three and a half years there at Quantiphi, and I am now doing my master's at San José State, working on how LLMs get served. It turns out the unglamorous layer is where a lot of the interesting problems are.
basics.now: Finishing my M.S. project on LLM serving and learning Go on the side.

work.name: Quantiphi
highlights: Built a self-service infrastructure platform adopted by 50 data engineers across 5 data platforms: a Python CLI and a Claude-on-Bedrock interface that turned plain-English requests into pre-approved Terraform and CloudFormation stacks, with approval gates and TTL teardown. Cut platform-team requests ~85% and dev spend ~18%.

Architected the migration of an Informatica-on-EC2 ETL platform to Lambda and ECS Fargate services orchestrated by Step Functions, ingesting change data from 8+ sources across 5 countries into Redshift. Authored the design and cost model (projected 70% lower compute) and mentored 2 juniors.
Split day-long full loads into restartable 2-hour batches, holding a T+1 freshness SLA on 95%+ of runs as volume doubled from 300 GB to 600 GB/day.
Enforced policy-as-code guardrails on 120 CloudFormation and Terraform stacks across 3 accounts with Control Tower, SCPs and Lambda checks; non-compliant stacks rolled back automatically.
On-call for 6 production services; consolidated 3 environments into one Grafana dashboard with symptom-based CloudWatch alerts, cutting MTTR from 3 hours to 10 minutes.

Shipped a major release every 2 weeks via Jenkins with two-layer rollback: CloudFormation reverted failed stack updates, and failed post-deploy checks redeployed the last known-good template and image.
story: I was on the platform team for a large insurer's data platform. Most of my time went to two things.

The first was moving the ETL off Informatica servers onto Lambda and Fargate, run by Step Functions. I wrote the design and the cost model and took it through review with the platform, data, business and finance people. On paper it cuts compute cost by about 70%. That is a projection, not a bill.

The part I liked most was smaller. Full loads took a whole day, so a failure late in the run meant starting over and hitting the source databases twice the next day. I split them into batches of about two hours that restart on their own, so a failure only reruns its own batch. We met the next-day deadline on 95%+ of runs while the data doubled to about 600 GB a day. Most of the misses came from other teams changing their source databases, which is a sentence I said in a lot of meetings.

The second was a self-service tool that let about fifty data engineers get their own test infrastructure by asking for it, with an LLM in the middle that was only allowed to fill in blanks. There is a longer write-up on it.

I was also on call for six services. Putting all three environments on one Grafana dashboard, with alerts on what users actually felt, took a typical fix from about three hours to about ten minutes. Releases went out every two weeks, and a release that failed its checks rolled itself back to the last version that worked. I mentored two junior engineers for a year and handed the platform over to a five-person support team.

work.name: Quantiphi
highlights: Authored CloudFormation and Terraform for 40 interdependent stacks per environment and built the platform network: segmented VPC subnets, NACLs, security groups and IAM isolation between team workloads.
Built and operated 30 daily ETL Lambdas per environment with run-locking, health checks and control-table backups, deployed through Jenkins pipelines with Trivy scanning.
Ran 5 types of disaster-recovery drill every 4 months; restored a failed production RDS instance in about an hour.
story: My first role was learning the platform by building it. I wrote the CloudFormation and Terraform for about forty stacks per environment, which depended on each other in ways you mostly find out about at deploy time. I also built the network that kept each team's workloads apart, and spent a fair share of my time working out why one service could not talk to another.

I ran about thirty ETL Lambdas a day per environment, and disaster-recovery drills every four months. So when a production database actually failed, restoring it from a snapshot took about an hour. I also moved a database to a new AWS account with no downtime, which was mostly careful preparation followed by one quick switch.

work.name: Quantiphi
highlights: Broke a monolithic ETL into event-driven microservices on Lambda, Step Functions and SQS, and ran containerised ETL workloads on ECS.
story: Before full time, I spent six months taking apart a monolithic ETL job and rebuilding it as small event-driven services on Lambda, Step Functions and SQS, with the heavier parts running as containers on ECS.

projects.name: driftfix
projects.title: driftfix
projects.badge: hackathon winner, then a team of three
projects.description: Finds manual AWS console changes that drifted from CloudFormation, has an LLM write the fix, and opens a pull request.
story: Someone fixes a production incident at 2 am by clicking around the AWS console, and nobody updates the template afterwards. On the next deploy CloudFormation quietly undoes the fix, and everyone gets to enjoy the same incident twice.

driftfix reads CloudTrail, works out what was changed by hand, asks an LLM on Bedrock to update the template, checks the result with cfn-lint and opens a pull request. It never touches infrastructure and never merges anything. A person still decides.

It started as Phantom, which won the AWS x Datadog GenAI hackathon. Three of us then rebuilt it properly as a multi-tenant service. I led that, and my part was the architecture, the Lambda pipeline, the cross-account IAM and the Terraform. In load tests ten stacks ran in parallel with zero errors. The slow part turned out to be the LLM, not us.

projects.name: cache-aware-scale-in
projects.title: Cache-aware scale-in
projects.description: A Kubernetes controller that tells the cluster which vLLM replica is cheapest to lose when scaling down.
story: When an LLM deployment scales down, Kubernetes has to pick a replica to delete, and it more or less picks the newest one. It has no idea that pod might be the one holding the cache everybody is using.
I wrote a small controller that scores each replica's cache and tells Kubernetes which one is cheapest to lose. You can try the difference below.

I have run the benchmark on three A100s. The controller removed the pod it was meant to, and it made no difference, because my test traffic warmed every replica's cache to about 95%. The fix is a harsher test and a better score, and that is what I am working on now.

projects.name: parallelized-nbody-simulation-cuda-cpp
projects.title: Parallel N-body simulation
projects.description: A galaxy simulation written five ways, from one CPU thread to tiled CUDA kernels, to compare them like for like.
story: A galaxy simulation that I wrote five different ways: one thread, OpenMP, Barnes-Hut, and two CUDA kernels. Same physics every time, so the only thing that changes is how the work is split up.

Along the way I found a data race in my own GPU kernel. Some bodies were feeling forces from the past and some from the future, which is not how gravity works. Splitting the update across two kernel launches fixed it.
The small galaxy below runs the same integrator in your browser. The GPU numbers are not measured yet.

projects.name: ai-sprint-planning-assistant
projects.title: AI sprint planning assistant
projects.description: Turns a planning spreadsheet into Jira tickets with a RAG pipeline and tool calls.
story: A hackathon project. You hand it a planning spreadsheet and it creates the Jira tickets, using a RAG pipeline to work out what goes where. Nobody enjoys copying rows into Jira.
It took first place out of about 50 teams at the Composio x Redis hackathon. There is no public repo for it yet.

projects.name: sdn-load-balance
projects.title: SDN load balancer
projects.description: An OpenFlow controller that load-balances HTTP traffic with five swappable algorithms.
story: An OpenFlow controller that spreads HTTP traffic across four servers. The controller picks a server for each new connection and writes the rule into the switch, so after the first packet the switch does the work on its own.
It has five algorithms you can swap, and I benchmarked all five with Locust. Pick one below and watch where the requests land.

projects.name: idempotent-order-cloud-api
projects.title: Duplicate-safe order ledger
projects.description: An order API where a retry never becomes a second order, even when retries arrive at the same instant.
story: If a client times out and sends the order again, you do not want to charge them twice. This API takes an idempotency key and guarantees exactly one order, however many times you hit send.
My first version looked correct and was not. Under parallel retries, 7 out of 20 test rounds returned a 500. The fix was a single INSERT ... ON CONFLICT, which is a lot less code than the bug was.
It runs on ECS Fargate with Postgres on RDS, all in Terraform. Go ahead and hammer the button.
